'''[[Olympique Lyonnais (Superleague Formula team)|Superleague
Formula]]''' }} }} '''Olympique Lyonnais''' ({{Langx|Fr|Olympique lyonnais}}; {{IPA|fr|ɔlɛ̃pik ljɔnɛ}}), commonly referred to as simply '''Lyon''' ({{IPA|fr|ljɔ̃}}) or '''OL''', is a men's French professional [[association football|football]] club based in [[Lyon]], [[Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes]], [[France]]. With origins dating back to 1899, they were founded in 1950.{{cite web |title=Histoire de l'OL dates clés |url=https://www.ol.fr/en/first-team/history/histoire-de-lol-dates-cles |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210729161619/https://www.ol.fr/en/first-team/history/histoire-de-lol-dates-cles |archive-date=29 July 2021 |access-date=29 July 2021 |website=OL.fr |language=fr}} The club currently competes in [[Ligue 1]], the top division of [[Football in France|French football]]. They play their home matches at the 59,186-capacity [[Parc Olympique Lyonnais]], commercially known as the [[Groupama]] Stadium, in [[Décines-Charpieu]], a suburb in the [[Metropolis of Lyon]]. The club's home colours are white, red and blue. Lyon was a member of the [[G14 (football)|G14]] group of leading European football clubs and are founder members of its successor, the [[European Club Association]]. The club won its first [[Ligue 1]] championship in [[Division 1 2001–02|2002]], beginning a national record-setting streak of seven successive titles. Lyon has also won eight [[Trophée des Champions|Trophées des Champions]], five [[Coupe de France|Coupes de France]], and three [[Ligue 2]] titles. On a [[UEFA competitions|European level]], the team has participated in the [[UEFA Champions League]] seventeen times, reaching the semi-final of the competition during the [[2009–10 UEFA Champions League|2009–10 season]] and the [[2019–20 UEFA Champions League|2019–20 season]], and have made it to the quarterfinals in three other occasions. They have also qualified for the [[UEFA Europa League|Europa League]] numerous times, making it as far as the semi-final during the [[2016–17 UEFA Europa League|2016–17 season]].{{cite web |title=History: Lyon 3-1 Ajax |url=https://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/match/2019700--lyon-vs-ajax/ |publisher=UEFA |access-date=27 July 2025}} The club's nickname, ''Les Gones'', translates to "The Kids" in Lyon's regional [[dialect]] of [[Franco-Provençal]]. They have a long-standing rivalry with nearby team [[AS Saint-Étienne|Saint-Étienne]], against whom they contest [[Olympique Lyonnais–AS Saint-Étienne rivalry|Le Derby]]. Lyon was owned by French businessman [[Jean-Michel Aulas]] from June 1987 until it was purchased by American businessman [[John Textor]] in December 2022.{{cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/mikeozanian/2022/06/21/olympique-lyonnais-price-tag-for-john-textor-846-million/?sh=6ab20975678e|title=Olympique Lyonnais Price Tag For John Textor: $846 Million|work=Forbes|date=21 June 2022|access-date=23 June 2022|archive-date=23 June 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220623122843/https://www.forbes.com/sites/mikeozanian/2022/06/21/olympique-lyonnais-price-tag-for-john-textor-846-million/?sh=6ab20975678e|url-status=live}} [[Michele Kang]] was eventually announced president of the club in June 2025 following Textor's resignation from his leadership position due to the poor financial state of Lyon. ==History== [[File:Place des Terreaux - 2.JPG|right|thumb|[[Place des Terreaux]] was the place of celebration of honors of Olympique Lyonnais.]] {{main|History of Olympique Lyonnais}} '''Origin (1899–1950)''' In 1899, a football club named ''Olympique de Lyon'' was formed within the multi-sport club, [[Lyon Olympique|Lyon Olympique Universitaire]], originally formed in 1896 as ''Racing Club de Lyon''. During the early years of the club, the football section was often overshadowed by then-local rivals, [[FC Lyon]]. Following numerous internal disagreements regarding the cohabitation of amateurs and professionals within the club, then-manager of the club Félix Louot and his entourage contemplated forming their own club. Following months of meetings, Louot's plans came to fruition when a final meeting of around twenty people took place on 23 May 1950 in ''Café Neuf'' in the city's main square, [[Place Bellecour]]. During this meeting, the name ''Olympique Lyonnais'' was decided for the new club, as well as the club's colours of red and blue. Among the twenty people were Albert Trillat, credited with the club's name and colours, as well as Armand Groslevin, who would become the club's first president.{{cite web |title=#OL70 ANS: Le 26 Mai, La Naissance D'Un Noveau Club de Football À Lyon... L'Olympique Lyonnais |url=https://www.ol.fr/en/news/retro-il-y-a-70-ans-l-histoire-de-olympique-lyonnais-etait-lancee-2 |publisher=OL.fr |access-date=25 August 2024}} Days later on 26 May, Lyon-based newspaper, ''[[Le Progrès]]'' reported that the club had officially been formed. ===Early success (1950–1987)=== On 27 August 1950, the club played its first official match under manager [[Oscar Heisserer]], defeating [[CA Paris-Charenton]] 3–0 in front of 3,000 supporters, with Lyon's first goal being scored within the first forty seconds of the match.{{cite web |title=70 years ago, on August 27, 1950, OL played the first match in its history |url=https://www.ol.fr/en/news/70-years-ago-on-august-27-1950-ol-played-the-first-match-in-its-history#:~:text=On%20August%2027,%201950,%20at,lines%20of%20their%20great%20story. |publisher=Olympique Lyonnais |access-date=24 May 2025}} The majority of the players in Lyon's squad had previously played for Lyon Olympique Universitaire.{{cite web |title=70 years ago, on August 27, 1950, OL played the first match in its history |url=https://www.ol.fr/en/news/70-years-ago-on-august-27-1950-ol-played-the-first-match-in-its-history#:~:text=On%20August%2027,%201950,%20at,lines%20of%20their%20great%20story. |publisher=Olympique Lyonnais |access-date=24 May 2025}} In just the club's second year of existence, Lyon were crowned champions of [[Ligue 2|Division 2]] during the [[1950–51 French Division 2|1950–51 season]], securing promotion to [[Ligue 1|Division 1]] for the [[1951–52 French Division 1|1951–52 season]]. The club maintained its place in Division 1 for the remainder of the decade, excluding a year's stint in Division 2 for the [[1953–54 French Division 2|1953–54 season]]. Lyon achieved moderate success during the 1960s and 1970s with the likes of [[Fleury Di Nallo]], [[Néstor Combin]], [[Serge Chiesa]], [[Bernard Lacombe]] and [[Jean Djorkaeff]] playing major roles. Under manager [[Lucien Jasseron]], Lyon won its first-ever [[Coupe de France]] title defeating [[FC Girondins de Bordeaux|Bordeaux]] 2–0 during the [[1964 Coupe de France Final|1963–64 season]]. The club also performed respectably in the league under Jasseron's reign until the [[1965–66 French Division 1|1965–66 season]], when Lyon finished 16th, which ultimately led to Jasseron's departure. His replacement was [[Louis Hon]], who helped Lyon win their second Coupe de France title after defeating [[FC Sochaux-Montbéliard|Sochaux]] 3–1 during the [[1967 Coupe de France final|1966–67 season]].{{cite web |title=21 mai 1967, la touche finale du général |url=https://www.fff.fr/article/1046-21-mai-1967-la-touche-finale-du-general.html |publisher=Fédération Française de Football |access-date=24 May 2025}} Lyon was managed by former Lyon legend [[Aimé Mignot]] heading into the 1970s. Under Mignot's helm, Lyon won its third Coupe de France title during the [[1973 Coupe de France final|1972–73 season]], beating [[FC Nantes|Nantes]] 2–1.{{cite web |title=#OL70YEARS one day, one season: 1972-73 |url=https://www.ol.fr/en/news/ol70ans-un-jour-une-saison-1972-73-2 |publisher=Olympique Lyonnais |access-date=24 May 2025}} ===Jean-Michel Aulas' presidency (1987–2023)=== In June 1987, Lyon was bought by local [[Rhône (department)|Rhône]]-based businessman, [[Jean-Michel Aulas]] who took control of the club aiming to turn Lyon into an established Division 1 side. His ambitious plan, titled ''OL – Europe'', was designed to develop the club at a [[UEFA|European level]] and back into the first division within a period of no more than four years.{{cite web |title=Aulas, 36 years of presidency, thank you for everything |url=https://www.ol.fr/en/news/jean-michel-aulas-36-years-of-presidency-thank-you-for-everything |publisher=Olympique Lyonnais |access-date=24 May 2025}} The first manager under the new hierarchy was [[Raymond Domenech]]. The aspiring chairman gave Domenech ''[[blank cheque|carte blanche]]'' to recruit whoever he saw fit to help the team reach the first division. They went on to accomplish this in Domenech's first season in charge, qualifying for the [[UEFA Europa League|UEFA Cup]]. For the remainder of his tenure, however, the club underachieved. Domenech was replaced by former [[France national football team|French international]] [[Jean Tigana]], who led the team to an impressive second place in the [[1994–95 Division 1|1994–95 season]]. At the start of the new [[millennium]], Lyon began to achieve greater success in [[French football]]. The club established itself as the premiere club in France, becoming France's richest club. Lyon also became known for developing promising talent who went on to achieve greatness not only in France, but also abroad and [[FIFA|internationally]]. Notable examples include [[Michael Essien]], [[Florent Malouda]], [[Sidney Govou]], [[Juninho Pernambucano|Juninho]], [[Cris (footballer, born 1977)|Cris]], [[Eric Abidal]], [[Mahamadou Diarra]], [[Patrick Müller (footballer)|Patrick Müller]] and [[Karim Benzema]]. Lyon won its first ever Ligue 1 title in [[2001–02 Division 1|2002]], starting a national record-breaking streak of seven successive titles. During that run, the club also won its fourth [[2008 Coupe de France Final|Coupe de France title]] in a 1–0 win over [[Paris Saint-Germain FC|Paris Saint-Germain]], its first [[2001 Coupe de la Ligue Final|Coupe de la Ligue title]] and six [[Trophée des Champions]]. The club also performed well in UEFA competitions, reaching as far as the quarter-finals on three occasions and the semi-finals in 2010 in the [[UEFA Champions League]]. Lyon's streak and [[Dynasty (sports)|consistent dominance]] of [[French football]] came to an end during the [[Ligue 1 2008–09|2008–09 season]], when it lost the title to [[FC Girondins de Bordeaux|Bordeaux]]. Several years later, during the [[2012 Coupe de France final|2011–12 season]], Lyon won their fifth and most recent Coupe de France trophy in a 1–0 victory against [[US Quevilly-Rouen Métropole|Quevilly]].{{cite web |title=Rétro: 8 years ago, OL won their 5th Coupe de France |url=https://www.ol.fr/en/news/retro-il-y-a-8-ans-l-ol-remportait-sa-5eme-coupe-de-france-2 |publisher=Olympique Lyonnais |access-date=1 June 2025}} Lyon began investment in sports outside of football, operating an [[esports]] team in China,{{cite web |url=https://equalizersoccer.com/2019/08/22/nwsl-expansion-merritt-paulson-says-two-teams-2020-one-2021-west-coast-southeast-mls-usl/ |title=Paulson says NWSL has three new teams committed for next two seasons |first=Jeff |last=Kassouf |publisher=The Equalizer |date=22 August 2019 |access-date=15 September 2019 |archive-date=23 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191023075026/https://equalizersoccer.com/2019/08/22/nwsl-expansion-merritt-paulson-says-two-teams-2020-one-2021-west-coast-southeast-mls-usl/ |url-status=live}} and in 2019 purchased a minority stake in the local [[ASVEL Basket|ASVEL]] [[basketball]] club, specifically purchasing a 25% interest in ASVEL's men's side and a 10% interest in the [[ASVEL Féminin|women's side]].{{cite news |url=http://www.sportspromedia.com/news/olympique-lyonnaislyon-asvel-french-soccer-basketball-investment |title=Lyon seal €3.7m Asvel investment deal |magazine=SportsPro |date=24 June 2019 |access-date=15 September 2019 |archive-date=24 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190624133730/http://www.sportspromedia.com/news/olympique-lyonnaislyon-asvel-french-soccer-basketball-investment |url-status=live }} The club later announced in December of the same year that it would buy an 89.5% stake in the U.S. [[National Women's Soccer League]] team known at the time as Reign FC. The purchase closed in January 2020 following approval of the NWSL board.{{cite press release |url=http://www.nwslsoccer.com/news/article/ol-groupe-to-become-majority-owner-of-national-womens-soccer-leagues-reign-fc |title=OL Groupe to become majority owner of National Women's Soccer League's Reign FC |publisher=National Women's Soccer League |date=19 December 2019 |access-date=19 December 2019 |archive-date=5 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230405034158/https://www.nwslsoccer.com/news/article/ol-groupe-to-become-majority-owner-of-national-womens-soccer-leagues-reign-fc |url-status=dead }} Several weeks later, the rebranding of Reign FC as [[OL Reign]] was announced.{{cite press release |url=https://www.olreign.com/news/2020/3/6/reign-fc-reveal-new-name-and-brand-identity |title=Reign FC Reveal New Name and Brand Identity |publisher=OL Reign |date=6 March 2020 |access-date=12 March 2020 |archive-date=9 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220409085253/https://www.olreign.com/news/2020/3/6/reign-fc-reveal-new-name-and-brand-identity |url-status=dead }} In the [[2019-20 Ligue 1|2019–20 season]], Lyon suffered a poor start to the season, and ended the season in seventh place, as the league was cancelled due to the coronavirus outbreak. Lyon also reached the final of the [[Coupe de la Ligue]], however, they eventually lost to [[Paris Saint-Germain F.C.|Paris Saint-Germain]] 6–5 on penalties.{{Cite news |date=31 July 2020 |title=PSG complete domestic treble with League Cup triumph |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/uk-soccer-france-psg-lyo-report-idUKKCN24W38W |access-date=5 May 2023 |archive-date=5 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230505020511/https://www.reuters.com/article/uk-soccer-france-psg-lyo-report-idUKKCN24W38W |url-status=live }} Ultimately, this meant that Lyon failed to qualify for European competition for the first time in 24 years. tournaments.{{cite web |title=Ligue 1: Former Interim Coach Pierre Sage Aims for Longevity at Lyon removed and he was named the new permanent coach.{{cite web |url=https://onefootball.com/en/news/lyon-appoint-pierre-sage-as-new-permanent-head-coach-39712984 |title=Lyon appoint Pierre Sage as new permanent head coach |last=Buxton |first=Richard |work=Onefootball |date=3 July 2024 |access-date=22 January 2025}} On 27 January 2025, Sage was sacked as Lyon manager and replaced by Portuguese coach |url=https://ligue1.com/articles/l1_article_1796-paulo-fonseca-joins-lyon-habib-beye-appointed-at-rennes |access-date=31 January 2025}} Fonseca eventually led Lyon to a 6th place finish, qualifying |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/article/lyon-qualified-europa-league-following-212000414.html |publisher=Yahoo! Sports |access-date=1 June 2025}} During this period, the club sold its women's team, [[OL Lyonnes]], known at the time as ''Olympique Lyonnais Féminin'' as well as the [[LDLC Arena]], a multipurpose arena near Lyon's stadium.{{cite web |last1=Entwistle |first1=Luke |title=Lyon thought they were too big to fail. Now they face a season in Ligue 2 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2025/jun/26/lyon-fail-season-ligue-2-great-football-club |work=The Guardian |date=26 June 2025 |access-date=2 July 2025}} On 24 June 2025, Lyon were administratively relegated to [[Ligue 2]] by the [[Direction Nationale du Contrôle de Gestion|DNCG]] due to the poor state of the club's finances.{{cite web |title=Lyon relegated: French club demoted to Ligue 2 over finances |date=24 June 2025 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cy7ng4vj8leo |publisher=BBC Sport |access-date=27 June 2025}} ===Michele Kang's presidency (2025–present)=== On 30 June 2025, it was announced that OL Lyonnes president and shareholder in [[OL Groupe]], [[Michele Kang]], had been appointed as Chairwoman and CEO of OL Groupe and President of Olympique Lyonnais, with Michael Gerlinger also being appointed Director General after John Textor resigned from his leadership positions.{{cite web |title=Eagle Football Group – Michele King appointed as Chairwoman and President of Olympique Lyonnais |url=https://www.actusnews.com/en/eagle-football-group/pr/2025/06/30/michele-kang-appointed-as-chairwoman-and-president-of-olympique-lyonnais |publisher=Actusnews |access-date=30 June 2025}} Just over two weeks later, on 9 July 2025, the decision to relegate Lyon due to financial problems was reversed due to actions made by the club, allowing Lyon to compete in both Ligue 1 and the Europa League for the [[2025–26 Ligue 1|2025–26 season]].{{cite web |title=L'OL reste en Ligue 1 |url=https://www.ol.fr/fr/actualites/l-ol-reste-en-ligue-1 |publisher=Olympique Lyonnais |language=fr |access-date=9 July 2025}} On 23 June 2026, Eagle Bidco, represented by its judicial administrator [[Cork Gully]], reached an agreement with Michele Kang for the acquisition of 87.8% of the capital of Eagle Football Group, the parent company of Olympique Lyonnais. As part of the agreement, Kang committed to buying out the group's main lenders' debt and to injecting up to €71 million (€75 million including transaction costs) into the group, including €31 million upon completion, as part of a wider restructuring aimed at stabilising the club's finances.{{cite web |url=https://www.ol.fr/fr/actualites/accord-en-vue-d-un-rachat-de-l-olympique-lyonnais-par-michele-kang |title=Accord en vue d’un rachat de l’Olympique Lyonnais par Michele Kang |publisher=Olympique Lyonnais |language=fr |date=23 June 2026 }} Three days later, the acquisition was officially completed, making Kang the club's majority owner, while [[Matthieu Louis-Jean]] was appointed as Lyon's sporting director.{{cite web |url=https://www.ol.fr/fr/actualites/michele-kang-est-desormais-officiellement-la-nouvelle-proprietaire-de-l-ol-et-nomme-matthieu-louis-jean-directeur-sportif |title=Michèle Kang est désormais officiellement la nouvelle propriétaire de l'OL et nomme Matthieu Louis-Jean directeur sportif |publisher=Olympique Lyonnais |language=fr |date=26 June 2026 }} ==Ownership and finances== Olympique Lyonnais was owned by [[Rhône (department)|Rhône]] businessman [[Jean-Michel Aulas]], who acquired the club on 15 June 1987. He serves as the founder and chief operating officer of CEGID (Compagnie Européenne de Gestion par l'Informatique Décentralisée). After ridding the club of its debt, Aulas restructured the club's management and reorganised the finances and, in a span of two decades, transformed the club from a second division team into one of the richest football clubs in the world. However, Aulas has been lambasted by critics for running the club as if it were a business. During this period, the club's [[holding company]] operated on the [[Euronext|European Stock Exchange]] under the name [[OL Groupe]], initialled OLG.{{cite web | title=OL Groupe | url=http://www.euronext.com/quicksearch/resultquicksearch-2986-EN.html?matchpattern=OLG&entryType=symbol | archive-url=https://archive.today/20120729074114/http://www.euronext.com/quicksearch/resultquicksearch-2986-EN.html?matchpattern=OLG&entryType=symbol | url-status=dead | archive-date=29 July 2012 | publisher=Euronext | date=31 October 2009 | access-date=31 October 2009 }} Aulas currently serves on the board for the [[European Club Association]], a sports organisation representing [[Association football|football]] clubs in Europe. He was also the last president of the now-defunct [[G-14]] organisation. In April 2008, business magazine ''[[Forbes]]'' ranked Lyon as the thirteenth most valuable football team in the world. The magazine valued the club at $408 million (€275.6M), excluding debt.{{cite web | title=Soccer Team Valuations | url=https://www.forbes.com/lists/2008/34/biz_soccer08_Soccer-Team-Valuations_Rank.html | work=Forbes | date=30 April 2008 | access-date=11 November 2008 | archive-date=29 January 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110129025737/http://www.forbes.com/lists/2008/34/biz_soccer08_Soccer-Team-Valuations_Rank.html | url-status=live }} In February 2009, Lyon were rated in the 12th spot in the [[Deloitte Football Money League]], reportedly bringing in an annual revenue of €155.7 million for the [[2007–08 Ligue 1|2007–08 season]], which ranks among the world's best football clubs in terms of revenue.{{cite web | title=English clubs dominate 2009 Money League | url=http://fourfourtwo.com/news/england/24940/default.aspx | publisher=FourFourTwo | date=12 February 2009 | access-date=31 October 2009 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111003102403/http://fourfourtwo.com/news/england/24940/default.aspx | archive-date=3 October 2011 | url-status=dead }} In 2016, a Chinese private equity fund acquired 20% stake in Olympique Lyonnais Group for €100 million. The fund was managed by [[IDG Capital|IDG Capital Partners]].{{cite web|url=https://www.actusnews.com/documents_communiques/ACTUS-0-45357-OLG-120816-Press-release-GB.pdf|title=OL Groupe announces the proposed acquisition of 20% of its share capital by the Chinese investment fund IDG Capital Partners|date=12 August 2016|access-date=15 August 2016|publisher=Olympique Lyonnais Group|archive-date=15 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211215212823/https://www.actusnews.com/documents_communiques/ACTUS-0-45357-OLG-120816-Press-release-GB.pdf|url-status=live}} In December 2022, American businessman [[John Textor]] completed the purchase of the club, owning 77.49% of the club's shares and thus becomes the new owner of the club. Under this arrangement, the club suggested that Aulas would continue to serve as president for at least three more seasons.{{Cite web|url=https://www.olympique-et-lyonnais.com/ol-rachat-jean-michel-aulas-va-encore-garder-la-main-trois-ans,260798.html|title=OL - Rachat : Jean-Michel Aulas va encore garder la main trois ans|date=21 June 2022|language=fr|access-date=26 February 2023|archive-date=26 February 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230226062512/https://www.olympique-et-lyonnais.com/ol-rachat-jean-michel-aulas-va-encore-garder-la-main-trois-ans,260798.html|url-status=live}} However, on 8 May 2023, it was announced that Textor had replaced Aulas to become the chairman and CEO of OL Groupe, thus making him the new president of Olympique Lyonnais, ending Aulas' 36 years rule, during which more than 50 major titles have been won for both men's and women's teams.{{Cite web|url=https://www.ol.fr/fr/actualites/communique-de-presse-nouvelle-gouvernance-pour-olympique-lyonnais-groupe|title=Communiqué de presse : Nouvelle gouvernance pour Olympique Lyonnais Groupe|date=8 May 2023|publisher=Olympique Lyonnais|language=fr|access-date=8 May 2023|archive-date=19 May 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230519204203/https://www.ol.fr/fr/actualites/communique-de-presse-nouvelle-gouvernance-pour-olympique-lyonnais-groupe|url-status=live}} Jean-Michel Aulas was appointed honorary chairman, and ''L'Équipe'' reported that Aulas would be compensated €10 million for his exit and retain a 9% stake in the club.{{cite news |url=https://apnews.com/article/lyon-jean-michel-aulas-textor-dfa8c59733120758576c33eb9904a129 |title=End of an era: Jean-Michel Aulas leaves French club Lyon |date=8 May 2023 |access-date=8 May 2023 |work=[[Associated Press]] |first=Samuel |last=Petrequin |archive-date=20 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230520023606/https://apnews.com/article/lyon-jean-michel-aulas-textor-dfa8c59733120758576c33eb9904a129 |url-status=live }} On 13 July 2023, Frenchman Santiago Cucci was named to become the new interim executive president of [[OL Groupe]], but later resigned in November. He was replaced by Laurent Prud'homme, who remained in the position until May 2025.{{Cite web|url=https://www.ol.fr/en/news/santiago-cucci-becomes-interim-executive-president-of-olympique-lyonnais|title=Santiago Cucci becomes interim executive president of Olympique Lyonnais|date=13 July 2023|access-date=13 July 2023|archive-date=13 July 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230713184715/https://www.ol.fr/en/news/santiago-cucci-becomes-interim-executive-president-of-olympique-lyonnais|url-status=live}} Following Lyon's administrative relegation to [[Ligue 2]] in June 2025 by the [[DNCG]], John Textor resigned due to pressure from the club's shareholders. American businesswoman [[Michele Kang]], one of the club's shareholders and the owner of [[OL Lyonnes|Lyon women's team]], was appointed as the new president. In Lyon's appeal hearing with the DNCG on 9 July, represented by Michele Kang and the club's new general director Michael Gerlinger, the club won the appeal, and the DNCG confirmed that Lyon would remain in Ligue 1.{{cite web|url=https://www.lequipe.fr/Football/Actualites/L-ol-est-maintenu-en-ligue-1-par-la-dncg/1576740|title=L'OL est maintenu en Ligue 1 par la DNCG en appel|date=9 July 2025|publisher=L'Équipe}} {{updated|30 June 2025.}} {| class="wikitable" style="margin:auto; font-size:85%;" cellspacing="4" |- ! In 1910, the then-mayor of [[Lyon]], [[Édouard Herriot]], wanted to develop and build a [[Stadium|sports stadium]] with both an [[Track and field athletics|athletics]] track and a [[velodrome]] in the city.{{cite web |title=Matt Stadium (ex-Stade de Gerland) |url=https://www.lyon.fr/lieu/stade/matmut-stadium-ex-stade-de-gerland#:~:text=Le%20Stade%20de%20Gerland%2C%20construit,au%20début%20du%20XXe%20siècle. |publisher=Ville de Lyon |access-date=12 July 2025}} In 1912, the stadium was officially mandated and local architect [[Tony Garnier (architect)|Tony Garnier]] was given the reins in designing and constructing it. Construction began in 1914 with the hope that the stadium would be completed before the [[World's fair|International Exhibition of 1914]]. Construction was halted due to the [[World War I|First World War]], but construction was eventually completed in 1919. By 1920, the stadium was completely functional. In 1926, the Stade de Gerland, with a capacity of 35,000, was inaugurated by Herriot.{{cite web |title=Histoire du Stade Gerland |date=16 April 2019 |url=https://surlatouche.fr/histoire-du-stade-gerland/ |publisher=surlatouche.fr |access-date=12 July 2025}} In 1967, the stadium was listed as a [[Monument historique]]. As well as hosting Lyon's home games, the stadium hosted matches for the [[UEFA Euro 1984|Euro 1984]], [[1998 FIFA World Cup|1998 World Cup]] and the [[2003 FIFA Confederations Cup|2003 Confederations Cup]]. The stadium's cycling track was eventually removed to increase the seating capacity to around 50,000. In September 1980, the stadium would see its record attendance of 48,552 during a [[Olympique Lyonnais–AS Saint-Étienne rivalry|derby game]] between Lyon and [[AS Saint-Étienne|Saint-Étienne]].{{cite web |title=LOU: Stade Gerland & Affluences |date=21 May 2020 |url=https://surlatouche.fr/lou-stade-gerland-affluences/ |publisher=surlatouche.fr |access-date=12 July 2025}} In 1984, minor renovations were made to the stadium by architect René Gagis.{{cite web |title=Gerland Stadium |url=http://ol-fans.weebly.com/gerland-stadium.html |publisher=OL Fans |access-date=12 July 2025}} This included construction of the [[Jean Bouin]] and [[Jean Jaurès]] stands. Further renovations were needed to prepare the stadium for the [[1998 FIFA World Cup]], as by that time FIFA had mandated that all stadiums used for international matches had to be [[all-seater]]. These renovations, planned by architect Albert Constantin, included the Jean Jaurès and Jean Bouin stands being demolished and rebuilt as well as removing the remaining athletics track. This new incarnation of the stadium had a maximum capacity of 40,494. On 5 December 2015, Lyon played their final game in the Stade de Gerland in a 2–0 defeat against [[Angers SCO|Angers]].{{cite web |title=Il y a neuf ans l'OL jouait son dernier match de Ligue 1 à Gerland |date=5 December 2024 |url=https://madeingones.ouest-france.fr/infos/article-ol-il-y-a-neuf-ans-l-ol-jouait-son-dernier-match-de-ligue-1-a-gerland-465509.html |publisher=Made in Gones |access-date=12 July 2025}} The stadium is now the home of [[Lyon OU Rugby]] and currently holds a capacity of 35,000 spectators.{{cite web |title=Matmut x le LOU |url=https://www.lourugby.fr/matmut-x-le-lou |publisher=LOU Rugby |access-date=12 July 2025}} '''Parc Olympique Lyonnais (2016–present)''' On 1 September 2008, Lyon president Jean-Michel Aulas announced plans to create a new 60,000-seater stadium, tentatively called ''OL Land'', to be built on 50 hectares of land located in [[Décines-Charpieu]], a suburb of Lyon. Over a month later, on 13 October 2008, the project was agreed upon by the State, the [[General councils (France)|General Council of Rhône]], the [[Grand Lyon]], [[Lyon Metro|SYTRAL]] and the municipality of Décines-Charpieu for construction with approximately €180 million of public money being used, with between €60–80 million coming from the [[Urban Community of Lyon]].{{cite news |title=Le grand stade est relancé |url=http://www.football365.fr/france/infos-clubs/lyon/article_270702_lyon-ol-land-Le-grand-stade-est-relance.shtml |work=France Soir |language=fr |date=16 October 2008 |access-date=30 October 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110131041336/http://www.football365.fr/france/infos-clubs/lyon/article_270702_lyon-ol-land-Le-grand-stade-est-relance.shtml |archive-date=31 January 2011 |url-status=dead }} After the announcement, however, the club's efforts to get the stadium off the ground were hindered mainly due to slow administrative procedures, political interests and various opposition groups, who viewed the stadium as financially, ecologically and socially wrong for the taxpayers and community of Décines-Charpieu. The official name of the stadium was provisionally to be ''Le Stade des Lumières''.{{cite web |url=http://www.olweb.fr/en/team/new-stadium-167.html |title=New Stadium | Club | OLWeb.fr |access-date=25 [[File:Karim Benzema 17586.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Former Lyon player [[Karim Benzema]] training at the [[Centre Tola Vologe]].]] ==Training centre== {{Main|Centre Tola Vologe}} The [[Centre Tola Vologe]] was the training centre and club headquarters of Olympique Lyonnais before the move to their new stadium in 2016. It is located in the city of Lyon, not far from the Stade de Gerland. The facility is named after [[Anatole Vologe]], commonly called Tola Vologe, who was a Lyon [[Athlete|sportsman]] and was murdered by the [[Gestapo]] during World War II. The facility is known for its high-level training[http://www.lesdessousdusport.fr/dossiers/lyon-tola-vologe-127-1146-1 Lyon : Tola Vologe] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100213184203/http://www.lesdessousdusport.fr/dossiers/lyon-tola-vologe-127-1146-1|date=13 February 2010}} and several prominent players have passed through the youth training centre. These include [[Karim Benzema]], [[Hatem Ben Arfa]], [[Sidney Govou]], [[Alexandre Lacazette]], [[Samuel Umtiti]] and [[Ludovic Giuly]]. The centre used to host training sessions for the senior team and also served as the home facility for the club's [[Olympique Lyonnais Reserves and Academy|reserve]], youth (both male and female), and [[Olympique Lyonnais Féminin|female]] sides, who both played their home matches at the [[Stade de Gerland|Plaine des Jeux de Gerland]]. Jean-François Vulliez is the current director of the centre. Both the men and women teams now train within a modern complex right by the new [[Parc Olympique Lyonnais|Groupama Stadium]] in [[Décines-Charpieu|Décines]]. The youth Academy also moved to the neighbouring town of [[Meyzieu]]. ==Colours and kits== {{Football kit box | | pattern_la = | pattern_b = _redbluevertical | pattern_ra = | leftarm = FFFFFF | body = FFFFFF | rightarm = FFFFFF | shorts = FFFFFF | socks = FFFFFF | title = Lyon won six of their seven league titles wearing this kit.}} Since the club's foundation, the primary colours have been red, blue, and white, with the latter being the most predominant of the three. During the early years of the club's existence, Olympique Lyonnais primarily played in all-white uniforms. In 1955, Lyon officials decided to add a red and blue [[chevron (insignia)|chevron]] and blue shorts to the combination.{{cite news|title=OL 1955–1960|url=http://www.fanfoot51.com/dessins%20maillots/Lyon/ol55.html|work=Fan Foot|date=21 November 2009|access-date=21 November 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120311001157/http://www.fanfoot51.com/dessins%20maillots/Lyon/ol55.html|archive-date=11 March 2012}} In 1961, the chevron tradition was disbanded and the two strips of red and blue were shaped horizontally.{{cite news|title=OL 1960–1965|url=http://www.fanfoot51.com/dessins%20maillots/Lyon/ol60.html|work=Fan Foot|date=21 November 2009|access-date=21 November 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120311001249/http://www.fanfoot51.com/dessins%20maillots/Lyon/ol60.html|archive-date=11 March 2012}} After six years, the club returned to the all-white uniforms, but kept intact the red and blue stripes, but, instead of keeping them horizontally, inserted them vertically and on the left side of the shirt.{{cite news|title=OL 1970–1975|url=http://www.fanfoot51.com/dessins%20maillots/Lyon/ol70.html|work=Fan Foot|date=21 November 2009|access-date=21 November 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110710224418/http://www.fanfoot51.com/dessins%20maillots/Lyon/ol70.html|archive-date=10 July 2011}} Lyon began wearing the shirt during the [[1970–71 French Division 1|1970–71 season]] and wore the kits up until the [[1975–76 French Division 1|1975–76 season]]. For the [[2002–03 Ligue 1|2002–03 season]], chairman Jean-Michel Aulas announced that the club would return the kits. Lyon wore them, with several different modifications every year, for six of their seven consecutive titles. In 1976, the club endured a drastic change to their kits, ditching the all-white uniforms for an all-red style, akin to English club [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]]. The club wore the kits up until the [[1989–90 French Division 1|1989–90 season]], with the [[1977–78 French Division 1|1977–78]] and [[1978–79 French Division 1|1978–79 seasons]] being excluded due to the club adding navy blue vertical stripes to the shirt that was deemed unsuccessful.{{cite news|title=OL 1975–1980|url=http://www.fanfoot51.com/dessins%20maillots/Lyon/ol75.html|work=Fan Foot|date=21 November 2009|access-date=21 November 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090815052526/http://www.fanfoot51.com/dessins%20maillots/Lyon/ol75.html|archive-date=15 August 2009}} Following the 1989–90 season, the club returned to the all-white kits and, at the start of the [[Division 1 1995–96|1995–96 season]], the club returned the vertical stripes, but opted to insert them in the center of the shirt, instead of to the left. The club kept this style until the [[2001–02 Division 1|2001–02 season]]. For the [[2009–10 Ligue 1|2009–10 season]], Lyon returned the horizontal red and blue stripes. In the [[UEFA Champions League|Champions League]], Lyon has used a variety of different colours as first choice, including red, navy blue, light blue, black, silver and fluorescent yellow.{{cite web |url=http://www.colours-of-football.com/colours03/fra/lyon/lyon_2.html |title=Olympique Lyonnais 2 |publisher=Colours-of-football.com |access-date=21 August 2017 |archive-date=21 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170821084727/http://www.colours-of-football.com/colours03/fra/lyon/lyon_2.html |url-status=live }} ==Supporters== [[File:Before Olympique lyonnais - Real Madrid match-modified.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|Tribune of ''Bad Gones'' before the match Olympique Lyonnais – Real Madrid in 2006.]] {{citation needed span|date=June 2026|Olympique Lyonnais has an active fanbase composed of many groups of supporters. One of the club's most notable supporters group is ''Bad Gones'' ("Bad Kids"). The ''Bad Gones'' were established in 1987 around the time of Jean-Michel Aulas's purchase of the team and used to occupy the Virage Nord area of the Stade de Gerland, and currently occupy the Virage Nord area of the Parc Olympique Lyonnais. During the [[2007–08 Ligue 1|2007–08 season]], the group celebrated its 20th anniversary. The ''Bad Gones'' is the biggest group of supporters in France and have a very strong reputation in Europe, due to the club's control of [[Ligue 1]], as well as Lyon's continued appearances in the [[UEFA Champions League]].}} {{citation needed span|date=June 2026|Another notable supporters group is the ''Cosa Nostra Lyon'', who occupy the Virage Sud area of the stadium. The group was created in 2007 as a result of a merger between two groups, the ''Lugdunums'', which had existed since 1993 and ''Nucleo Ultra'', which formed in 2000. The merger was created to achieve a sense of stability among supporters. The group is no longer recognised by the club, but continues to operate in a functional manner. Other support groups include the ''Hex@gones'', which was formed in 2000 and sit in the Virage Sud area, the ''Gastrogones'', who occupy the [[Jean Bouin]] stand, and the ''O'Elles Club'', who sit in the [[Jean Jaurès]] stand.}} {{citation needed span|date=June 2026|The club also has support groups that are based in areas outside of the city of Lyon. The ''Gones 58'' supporters come from the department of [[Nièvre]] in [[Bourgogne]], while ''Gones 26'' origins come from the department of [[Drôme]] in nearby [[Valence, Drôme|Valence]]. Three minor support groups in ''Septimagones'', ''Loups Marchois'', and ''Dauphigones'' comes from the commune of [[Hérépian]], the department of [[Creuse]], and the department of [[Isère]], respectively. Outside of France, the ''Lyondoners'' are based in [[London]] and follow Lyon at home, away and internationally.}} ===Hooliganism, far-right and racist incidents=== Olympique Lyonnais has been repeatedly associated with some of the most serious episodes of fan violence and discriminatory behaviour in French football, a record that has drawn condemnation from club officials, governing bodies, and national politicians alike. Issues amongst club supporters are traceable to the late 1980s and the founding of the Bad Gones ultras group in 1987, whose early members openly displayed white supremacist imagery, including a [[Celtic Cross#White supremacist symbolism|Celtic cross symbol]] on one of the group's first scarves, and who were known at the time for racist and antisemitic acts.{{cite news |last=Lefèvre |first=Florian |date=21 January 2024 |title=At Olympique Lyonnais, a nationalist atmosphere persists in the stands |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/sports/article/2024/01/21/at-olympique-lyonnais-a-nationalist-atmosphere-persists-in-the-stands_6452950_9.html |work=[[Le Monde]] |access-date=25 June 2026}} In December 2008, three and a half hours before a Ligue 1 match between Lyon and Marseille, around a dozen supporters from each side met for a planned confrontation near the Ninkasi bar close to the Gerland stadium, before a group of around fifty people led by a figure from the Cosa Nostra supporters' group attempted to provoke further clashes outside the ground. A fight later broke out inside the stadium's south stand, resulting in two arrests, one of whom was found to be carrying a knife.{{cite news |last=Lamy |first=William |date=29 April 2010 |title=Supporters/club : la difficile cohabitation |url=https://www.lyoncapitale.fr/actualite/supporters-club-la-difficile-cohabitation |work=Lyon Capitale |language=fr |access-date=25 June 2026}} As of the start of 2009, Olympique Lyonnais had 18 active stadium bans, and was listed in a 2007 Senate information report alongside clubs including Saint-Etienne, Nice, Marseille, Paris, Lille, and Bordeaux as having "permanent overflows" of supporter violence, despite the club's public position that the level of violence at the Gerland was among the lowest in France. Police at the time estimated that approximately fifty members of the Cosa Nostra group could be classified as hooligans. One Cosa Nostra member was arrested and convicted during a derby against Saint-Etienne for wearing a jersey bearing the text "Adolf 88" and waving a flag associated with Italian fascism. ====2010s==== In April 2010, the French Ministry of the Interior ordered the dissolution of seven French supporter groups for violence, among them the Cosa Nostra Lyon. In 2011, several members of the Mezza Lyon hooligan group, which regularly frequented the south stand of the Groupama Stadium, vandalised and spray-painted neo-Nazi slogans on the premises of Magic Fans, a supporters' group of rival club AS Saint-Etienne.{{cite news |last=Lefèvre |first=Florian |date=21 January 2024 |title=At Olympique Lyonnais, a nationalist atmosphere persists in the stands |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/sports/article/2024/01/21/at-olympique-lyonnais-a-nationalist-atmosphere-persists-in-the-stands_6452950_9.html |work=Le Monde}} In April 2017, crowd disorder marred Lyon's Europa League quarter-final against Besiktas at the Parc OL. Around twenty minutes before kick-off, Lyon supporters spilt onto the pitch for their own safety as fireworks were set off and projectiles were thrown from an upper section housing the visiting supporters, delaying the game by 45 minutes. Lyon's director of security stated that around fifty Turkish fans had forced their way into the stadium. However, some Lyon supporters also sought confrontations with their Turkish counterparts outside and inside the ground.{{cite news |date=14 April 2017 |title=Lyon say they are 'victims' of Besiktas hooligans as investigation begins |url=https://www.espn.com/soccer/story |work=[[Associated Press]] |access-date=25 June 2026}} The incident resulted in Lyon receiving a suspended two-year ban from European competition.{{cite news |date=19 March 2018 |title=Lyon face European ban after Uefa charge while on suspended ban |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/football/43456844 |work=[[BBC Sport]] |access-date=25 June 2026}} In March 2018, up to 150 hooded Lyon supporters launched a premeditated attack on an anti-terrorist police unit outside the Groupama Stadium before the Europa League tie against [[CSKA Moscow]], leaving at least eight officers injured.{{cite news |date=16 March 2018 |title=Lyon condemn 'intolerable and premeditated' attacks on police by fans |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/football/43427595 |work=[[BBC Sport]] |access-date=25 June 2026}} The club condemned the attacks as "intolerable and premeditated" and acknowledged they were "detrimental" to the club, while pledging to work with police to identify those responsible. UEFA subsequently charged Lyon over racist behaviour, with a French sports publication reporting that the charges related to Nazi symbols displayed inside the stadium, Nazi salutes, and an attack on a non-white spectator, all while the club's suspended European ban remained in place.{{cite news |agency=AFP |date=19 March 2018 |title=Lyon soccer team charged with 'racist behavior' over Nazi symbols at game |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/lyon-soccer-team-charged-with-racist-behavior-over-nazi-symbols-at-game/ |work=[[Times of Israel]] |access-date=25 June 2026}} In September 2018, flyers were distributed among supporters in the Groupama Stadium's north end claiming that Marseille was "a city where AIDS reigns". Club president [[Jean-Michel Aulas]] called the material "ridiculous and odious" and consulted lawyers, though the club ultimately concluded it could not be legally prosecuted.{{cite news |last=Holyman |first=Ian |date=24 September 2018 |title=Lyon cannot prosecute fans for 'ridiculous and odious' Marseille slur |url=https://www.espn.com.sg/soccer/story/_/id/37562033/lyon-cannot-prosecute-fans-ridiculous-odious-marseille-slur |work=[[ESPN]] |access-date=25 June 2026}} That same month, a Lyon supporter was caught on camera making a Nazi salute during the Champions League game at Manchester City. The club announced it would seek to ban the individual for life.{{cite news |date=20 September 2018 |title=Police investigate apparent Nazi salute by Lyon fan at Manchester City |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2018/sep/20/police-investigate-apparent-nazi-salute-lyon-fan-manchester-city |work=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=25 June 2026}} Greater Manchester Police Prud'homme stated that such incidents "should no longer tarnish OL's image," an acknowledgement that the problem was systemic rather than isolated.{{cite news |date=20 January 2025 |title=Defeats, violence and shame: Lyon are at war with the rest of French football |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2025/jan/20/defeats-violence-and-shame-lyon-are-at-war-with-the-rest-of-french-football |work=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=25 June 2026}} The record of the fanbase became a political issue in early 2026, when Aulas entered the [[2026 Lyon municipal election]]. During a televised debate, he was challenged over accusations that he had tolerated violent and fascist individuals within Lyon's ultra groups during his time in charge, allegations he denied.{{cite news |last=Jucobin |first=Raphael |date=10 March 2026 |title=Jean-Michel Aulas ruffles feathers in Lyon after swapping football for politics |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/mar/10/jean-michel-aulas-lyon-mayor-race-football-politics |work=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=25 June 2026}} ==Statistics and records== {{further|List of Olympique Lyonnais players}} {| class="wikitable sortable" style="float:right; font-size:85%;" cellspacing="4" |- style="background:dimGrey;" ! Since the club's foundation in 1950, they have played over 50 seasons in [[Ligue 1|France's highest football division]], playing over 1,800 matches. Of the nine seasons the club played in [[Ligue 2]], they contested 310 matches. Lyon achieved their 1,000th victory during the [[2003–04 Ligue 1|2003–04 season]] after defeating [[RC Strasbourg Alsace|Strasbourg]]. The Moroccan-born French midfielder [[Serge Chiesa]] holds Lyon overall appearance record having played in 541 matches over the course of 14 seasons from 1969 to 1983. Following him is former [[Goalkeeper (association football)|goalkeeper]] [[Grégory Coupet]] who contested 518 matches over the course of 11 seasons from 1997 to 2008. Along with [[Sidney Govou]], Coupet also has the distinction of being the only player in Lyon's history to win all four domestic French titles having been a part of all seven Ligue 1 titles, the club's [[Coupe de France]] triumph in 2008, the only [[Coupe de la Ligue]] win in 2001, and six of the seven [[Trophée des Champions]] titles. Govou, Coupet, and [[Juninho Pernambucano|Juninho]] share the honour of being only Lyon players who were a part of all seven title runs. The club's all-time leading scorer is [[Fleury Di Nallo]], who scored 222 goals while at the club from 1960 to 1974. Di Nallo is also third behind Chiesa and Coupet in all time appearances having played in 489 matches during his 14-year stint at the club. Despite Di Nallo's impressive goalscoring record, he doesn't hold the record for most goals scored during a league season. That distinction was held by [[Bourg-en-Bresse]]-born [[André Guy]] who notched 25 goals, which he attained in the [[1968–69 French Division 1|1968–69 season]]. [[Alexandre Lacazette]], however, scored his 26th goal of the [[2014–15 Ligue 1|2014–15 league season]] in an important game away to [[Stade de Reims]] when he scored in the sixth minute. [[File:juninho-free-kick 2.jpg|thumb|300px|right|[[Juninho Pernambucano|Juninho]] converted a record 44 free kicks at Lyon]] Lyon's biggest victory is 10–0, which occurred of two occasions against [[AC Ajaccio|Ajaccio]] during the 1953–54 edition of the Coupe de France and, two seasons later, against [[Delle]] during the 1955–56 edition of the competition. Lyon's biggest league victory is 8–0 and also occurred on two occasions. The first being during the [[1966–67 French Division 1|1966–67 season]] against [[Angers SCO|Angers]], and the second being against Marseille during the [[Division 1 1997–98|1997–98 season]]. The club's biggest victory on the European stage occurred during the 1974–75 season, where Lyon hammered [[Luxembourg]]-based club [[FA Red Boys Differdange]] 7–0. ==Rivalries== {{Main|Olympique Lyonnais–AS Saint-Étienne rivalry|Choc des Olympiques}} Historically, Lyon has had a healthy rivalry with [[AS Saint-Étienne|Saint-Étienne]], head-to-head clashes between the clubs being referred to as the ''[[Olympique Lyonnais–AS Saint-Étienne rivalry|Derby rhônalpin]]''.{{cite news |title=Power struggle on the Rhone |url=https://www.fifa.com/classicfootball/stories/classicderby/news/newsid=1008724.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090803153941/http://www.fifa.com/classicfootball/stories/classicderby/news/newsid=1008724.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=3 August 2009 |work=[[FIFA|Fédération Internationale de Football Association]] |date=19 December 2009|access-date=3 August 2010}} Since the club's dominance at the start of the new millennium, however, they have established rivalries with [[Olympique de Marseille|Marseille]], [[FC Girondins de Bordeaux|Bordeaux]], [[Paris Saint-Germain F.C.|Paris Saint-Germain]] and [[Lille OSC|Lille]]. Lyon also share minor rivalries with fellow [[Rhône-Alpes]] clubs [[Grenoble Foot 38|Grenoble]] and [[AS Lyon Duchère]]. The Saint-Étienne rivalry began during the 1960s when Lyon established their residency in the French first division. The [[Arpitan]] rivalry stems simply from the close proximity of the clubs to each other, separated by just {{convert|38|mi|km|order=flip}}, as well as historical social and cultural difference between the two cities where they are based; Lyon traditionally cited as being a financially comfortable and middle class city, while [[Saint-Étienne]] is traditionally regarded as being more industrial and working-class. The [[local derby|derby]] also pits "the most recently successful French club" (Lyon) against "the formerly biggest French club" (Saint-Étienne) and is often seen as one of the high points of the [[Ligue 1]] season. Lyon's rivalry with Marseille goes back to 23 September 1945, when the clubs contested their first match. The derby, often called ''[[Choc des Olympiques]]'' ("Clash of the Olympics") or ''Olympico'', is often cited as being particularly important as both clubs are of high standard in [[French football]] and the championship is regularly decided between the two. Marseille, Saint-Étienne, Lyon, and PSG are the only French clubs to have won the French first division four straight times. ==Sponsors== On 7 August 2009, Lyon announced that it signed a ten-year deal with the German sportswear brand [[Adidas]], effective at the start of the [[2010–11 Ligue 1|2010–11 season]] with Lyon earning €5 million annually from the deal, plus possible royalty fees based on product sales.{{cite news|title=Olympique Lyonnais signed with Adidas |url=http://www.eufootball.biz/Sponsorship/7423-olympique_lyonnais_adidas_09.html |work=EU Football |date=14 August 2009 |access-date=31 October 2009 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090822113259/http://www.eufootball.biz/Sponsorship/7423-olympique_lyonnais_adidas_09.html |archive-date=22 August 2009 }} As of the [[2024–25 Ligue 1|2024–25 season]], Lyon still have a deal with Adidas which will last until the end of the 2028–29 season.{{cite web |first1=Susan |last1=Lingeswaran |title=Lyon renew kit supplier deal with Adidas until 2029 |url=https://www.sportcal.com/sponsorship/lyon-renew-kit-supplier-deal-with-adidas-until-2029/ |website=sportcal.com |date=8 February 2024 |access-date=6 October 2024}} Following the [[2008–09 Ligue 1|2008–09 season]], Lyon's long-term sponsorship agreement with the French [[multinational corporation]] [[Accor]] and Lyon-based [[Renault Trucks]] ended. On 22 July 2009, the Paris-based online bookmaker BetClic reached an agreement with Lyon to advertise on the club's kits. However, due to [[French law]] prohibiting [[online gambling]], Lyon could not wear its kits displaying the logo. On 12 August 2009, just before the opening league match against [[Le Mans FC|Le Mans]], the club was relieved of its BetClic-sponsored shirts by the [[Ligue de Football Professionnel]] (LFP), which warned the club that it risked forfeiting points if the club wore them.{{cite news|title=Olympique Lyonnais may take legal action against French league |url=http://www.eufootball.biz/Legal/7416-olympique_lyonnais_legal_action_french_league.html |work=EU Football |date=12 August 2009 |access-date=31 October 2009 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090830184644/http://www.eufootball.biz/Legal/7416-olympique_lyonnais_legal_action_french_league.html |archive-date=30 August 2009 }} Lyon complied and, since the Le Mans match, wore sponsorless shirts while playing on French soil. The deal lasted until the end of the [[2009–10 Ligue 1|2009–10 season]]. In 2010, the French ban on online gambling advertising was lifted and Lyon began wearing its BetClic-sponsored shirts on French soil. Lyon has the distinction of starting a national record-breaking streak of seven successive titles beginning with the [[2001–02 Division 1|2001–02 season]]. The club has also been crowned champions of [[Ligue 2]] three times, won five [[Coupe de France]] titles, one [[Coupe de la Ligue]] title and eight [[Trophée des Champions]]. Though the club is a regular participant in the [[UEFA Champions League]], they have only reached as far as the semi-finals, which was accomplished during the [[2009–10 UEFA Champions League|2009–10]] and [[2019–20 UEFA Champions League|2019–20]] seasons.
